title: The Programme Is Slipping
briefing: You lead 'Coldline 2', a 14-month controls programme across six sites: automated temperature alerting, logger downloads, contractor sign-off and driver fatigue rules. At month 7 it is 40% complete, and three site managers say they 'don't have time'.
The steering group meets on Thursday.

context.text: The logger fix from your control test is the one workstream already delivered.
The supplier criticality review you started has been folded into this programme, adding scope.

evidence.title: Programme status
evidence.body: Planned 58% complete by month 7; actual 40%. Northgate and Harrowgate on track; Eastfield, Corby Road and two others behind. Budget spent 52%.

evidence.title: Site managers' feedback
evidence.body: 'We get eleven programme emails a week.' 'Training clashes with peak shifts.' 'Nobody told us what's in it for the site.'

evidence.title: Sponsor
evidence.body: The COO sponsors the programme but has missed the last two steering groups.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for the slip?

options.label: The sites don't own the change: too much noise, training at the wrong times, no visible benefit, and an absent sponsor
The lagging site managers aren't committed
options.feedback: Blames people for a design problem; two sites are on track with the same programme.

options.label: Not enough budget
options.feedback: Spend (52%) is ahead of progress (40%): money isn't the constraint.

questions.prompt: What do you ask of the COO?

options.label: Attend Thursday, visit the two slowest sites with you, and make the programme a standing item in site managers' reviews
options.feedback: Specific, visible sponsorship that changes priorities on site.

options.label: Send an email to all sites supporting the programme
options.feedback: Another email adds to the noise.

options.label: Nothing: he's busy
options.feedback: A programme without an active sponsor loses to day-to-day pressure.

options.label: Prioritise the two workstreams with the biggest risk reduction (alerting, fatigue rules), move the rest by a quarter, cut communications to one weekly site note, and schedule training around peaks
options.feedback: Protects the risk outcomes, reduces load, and resets an achievable plan.

options.label: Keep the plan and escalate the lagging sites
options.feedback: Pushing harder on a plan the sites can't absorb deepens the slip.

options.label: Extend every workstream by six months
options.feedback: Avoids the hard choices; the highest-risk gaps stay open longer.

questions.prompt: How do you report status to the steering group?

options.label: Red overall, with the reasons, the replan, the risk impact of each delay, and the decisions you need from them
Amber: we're recovering
options.feedback: Watermelon reporting (green outside, red inside) destroys trust when it's found.

questions.prompt: How will you measure success from now on?

options.label: By risk outcomes: excursions caught before delivery, fatigue breaches, contractor visits verified, alongside milestones
options.feedback: Programmes exist to reduce risk, not to finish tasks.

lesson: Control programmes fail on adoption more than on design: active sponsorship, less noise, a focused replan and outcome measures recover them.
